catalog_quote: 1.1 Phonemes [...] The distinction between nasals is neutralised in final position, with their realisation as [m], [n] or [ŋ] apparently varying according to both phonological context and dialect. [...] Length is phonemic for all vowels [...] 1.2 Phonotactics. There are very few vowel-initial words. Syllables are generally open, though a word-final syllable can be closed by a nasal (and there are a few cases of medial nasal + consonant clusters). Clusters of vowels are rare; /ai/ and /ae/ are neutralised as [ai] (Mga [ai] ~ [e]), /au/ and /ao/ as [au]. 1.3 Stress. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable if a word ends in a vowel, on the ultimate if it ends in a consonant.
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is penultimate in vowel-final words and final in consonant-final words; since only a nasal may close a word-final syllable, this amounts to: stress the final syllable if it is closed (CVN), otherwise the penult. Right-edge, two-syllable window, final closed syllable counts as heavy.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in the sketch.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned. No statement about whether long vowels (phonemic length) attract stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word; no discussion of phrase-level prosody, clitics or citation forms. Sketch covers the inland dialect (Mabesi, Mariga) and is adapted from Lincoln's 1976 dissertation plus Ross's fieldnotes.
new_statements.identity_note: The Lynch & Ross 2002 sketch describes the inland dialect of Banoni as spoken at Mabesi (Lincoln 1976a data) and Mariga (Ross fieldnotes via Sr Mary Patricia); coastal vs inland dialect differences are noted but not described. Same language as Glottolog bann1247 'Bannoni' (WALS bnn).
